rv.q: Actors are agile and energetic, playing multiple parts and dancing or singing in interludes, although these feel latched on at times and sometimes performances feel slightly over-excitable.
There are also strange dreamlike sequences – like a dance rendition of ‘A Spoonful of Sugar’ which break up the narrative but don’t feel fully integrated into the play.
But while this swirling, muscular movement is visually arresting, it tends to diffuse rather than heighten the building tension.
Director Milli Bhatia could have honed and focused things better, but the performances are gregarious and attractive.
Despite its faults, Blue Mist is a must-see. And Dada a young playwright to watch out for.
It's funny, sarcastic, satirical, thought-provoking, informative, original. It has it all - except for a truly great ending.

Mohamed-Zain Dada's play touches on a range of urgent themes, notably the identity of young Asian men who, like many of their generation, feel squeezed to the margins both economically and culturally.
But while Blue Mist is a story that benefits from being seen from inside the world of the shisha lounge, this is also its drawback as a drama.
This is a stunning debut, linguistically brilliant, very funny, freighted with critique and truthful.
This ‘shisha lounge’ is well worth a visit.
Blue Mist is a strong playwriting debut that for the most part balances its serious point with very entertaining comic one-liners.

cn.t: Dada's vibrant debut about young British Muslim men in a London shisha lounge wins praise for its humor, energy, and challenge to stereotypes, though critics note the plot feels overstretched and unfocused at times.
